paper_title: Is activity-based working impacting health, work performance and perceptions? A systematic review
abstract: Numerous claims have been made about the benefits of activity-based working (ABW) on workers' health and work performance. Yet, it is unclear if these claims are proven. This systematic review aims to establish whether there is an evidence base for the effects of ABW on health, work performance and perceptions of the work environment. Eight databases were searched in September 2016. Three reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed the studies and extracted the data. Seventeen studies involving 36,039 participants were included. The study designs varied in rigorousness from qualitative studies to pre-post-trials and in sample size ranging from 12 to 11,799. This review found that ABW has positive merits in the areas of interaction, communication, control of time and space, and satisfaction with the workspace; however, it is unfavourable for concentration and privacy. For physical and mental health, the evidence is equivocal. ABW seems to be a promising concept that can be implemented and promoted based on some benefits for work performance and perceptions of the work environment when it is coupled with appropriate management support and organization. More high-quality research is needed to strengthen the evidence base further and establish its health effects.
methodology: Systematic review. Eight databases (Scopus, Pubmed, CINAHL, Business Source Complete, Health Business, PsychInfo, Embase, Web of Science) were searched in September 2016. Three reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text screening. Data extraction was performed by three co-authors. Included studies had to report an ABW intervention, be conducted in an office environment with adults, measure specific outcomes related to health, work performance, or perceptions of the physical/psychosocial work environment, and use pre-post, natural experiment, post-occupancy, or case study designs. Only peer-reviewed full-text articles in English were included. A quality assessment was performed based on study design, sample size, number of workplaces, statistical analyses, demographics, and response rates (scoring 3-13 points). The included studies comprised five pre-post-studies, eleven post-occupancy studies, and one qualitative study.
sample: 17 studies included, involving a total of 36,039 participants. Sample sizes of individual studies ranged from 12 to 11,799 participants.
manipulated_features: Activity-based working (ABW) environments, characterized by: employees not having an allocated desk or workspace; provision of a variety of tailored work environments (e.g., team desks, sit-stand workstations, quiet rooms, break-out areas, telephone and meeting rooms, lounge areas); non-territorial workplaces; workstation to employee ratio of 0.7-0.8; and sometimes 'hybrid' systems with allocated workstations plus extra activity-support spaces.
outcomes: Perceived influence of work area on health
Musculoskeletal discomfort and complaints (lower back, neck, shoulders, wrists/hands, legs)
Physical activity (accelerometer-assessed sedentary time, moderate-to-vigorous intensity, step counts, breaks in sedentary time)
Interactions (informal face-to-face conversations, group meetings, individual meetings)
Distractions (from conversations, sounds like doors, photocopiers, air-conditioning)
Perceptions of time and space control
Flexibility in working time and location
Access to, use of, and satisfaction with work location
Number of days working at home
Satisfaction with ambient conditions (glare, cold air)
Satisfaction with physical spaces for break and collaboration
key_findings: General health evidence is equivocal. One study found significantly lower general health scores in ABW at 16 months follow-up (p < 0.001). Two studies found no significant change in self-rated health. One study found a significantly smaller proportion of employees taking sick leave in flex office type (p < 0.05). ABW occupants had significantly more positive ratings on perceived influence of work area on health (p < 0.05). Employees with fixed desks were more likely to rate health negatively (32% vs 20%) than those in flexible spaces; uncomfortable furnishings showed a 49% increased likelihood of negatively rated health influences.

Musculoskeletal discomfort showed limited and mixed evidence. One study reported less lower back discomfort in ABW trial space (p < 0.05), but no changes in other body parts. Another study found general musculoskeletal discomfort significantly reduced after six months in new flexible office workspace with ergonomics training, and reduced discomfort in legs, wrists/hands among those with training.

Physical activity and sitting evidence is limited. Self-reported occupational sitting decreased (-14%) and standing increased (11%) in ABW trial space (p < 0.01). No significant differences in accelerometer-assessed sedentary or moderate-to-vigorous intensities. Increased workstation switches and time on the move were observed in ABW (not statistically tested).

Mental wellbeing (stress) showed mixed evidence. Employees in cell offices reported lower cognitive stress than all open-plan office types (p < 0.001). High need for concentration reported higher cognitive stress in all office types except cell and flexible offices (p < 0.05). No significant changes in stress levels after 16 months in ABW (p > 0.05).

Mental wellbeing (exhaustion/fatigue) evidence is limited. No difference in emotional exhaustion between office types (p > 0.05). No direct relationship between ABW and daily exhaustion. Working in ABW increased self-reported fatigue at 16 months follow-up (p < 0.01).

Communication, interactions, and collaboration showed emerging positive evidence. Five studies found positive associations with communication, nine with interactions, and two with collaboration. ABW environments better supported communication and cooperation, leading to significantly higher productivity in relation to these aspects. Communication was positively impacted over time. ABW was positively associated with engagement, enhanced connectivity, and effective/efficient communication. Overall satisfaction with communication opportunities increased, but communication with direct colleagues decreased, and difficulties discussing private issues in open spaces were noted.

Concentration showed mixed evidence. Two studies found positive effects or reduced distractions. Eight studies reported negative influence. Higher rated distraction in flex offices (3.30) compared to cell offices (2.69), but less than large open-plan offices (3.64). A slight increase in unwanted interruptions was found between fixed- and flexi-desk groups. Higher level of unwanted interruption in ABW compared to individual offices. Increased interruptions (email, phone calls) in NWW offices led to greater exhaustion. People in combi- or flex offices rated concentration less positively than individual/shared-room offices. 35% of respondents were satisfied with concentration opportunities in flex office.

Control (time and space) showed positive evidence. Higher perceptions of time and space control in ABW environments were reported in six studies. Significant increased access to, use, and satisfaction with work location, work hours, evening hours, home hours, and number of days working at home. Significant decrease in commute hours and office hours. Higher ratings of job control. All respondents associated NWW with greater job autonomy and flexibility in working time and location. Employees were less satisfied with lack of control of the office environment in flexible office plans compared to traditional, cellular offices.

Privacy showed mixed evidence. Four studies reported positive effects, seven reported negative effects. Significantly increased perception of privacy in intervention groups. Agile workspaces were good for confidential conversations and documents but considered less private than cellular offices. People in combi- or flex offices evaluated privacy negatively compared to individual/shared-room offices. Low satisfaction scores for privacy and lack of space for confidential phone calls were reported.

Work performance showed mixed evidence. Eight studies reported positive effects, three negative, and four no effect. Five studies found work productivity improved in ABW. Higher scores on productivity in ABW vs. hive or cell offices. Two studies reported improvement in job motivation/engagement. Higher job satisfaction for workers in shared-room and flex (ABW) offices vs. open plan. Perceived work ability fell significantly after reoccupying standard open-plan office after an ABW trial.

Satisfaction with the physical workspace was generally positive. Six studies found satisfaction with building aesthetics/architecture. Occupants were satisfied with the functionality of workspaces. Two studies found satisfaction with physical spaces for break and collaboration, while one found the opposite. Clear consensus on insufficient storage in ABW environments. Mixed reports on IT facilities and indoor environmental quality (satisfied with light/ventilation, but increased noise distractions and poor temperature control). Flex office users were less satisfied with indoor climate than individual/shared rooms. Occupants were significantly more satisfied with the ergonomic environment in intervention groups.
mechanisms: ABW supports collaboration through the provision of diverse spaces like break-out areas and cafes. The greater control over where and when tasks are performed in ABW environments, coupled with a supportive management style, contributes to improved work performance and satisfaction. The ability to regulate social interactions through different workstation types is also a proposed mechanism for control and privacy.
limitations: Diversity of disciplines and variation in research methods make it hard to draw solid conclusions.
Pre-post-studies are often limited in scale.
Post-only studies, while having large samples, provide weaker evidence of causality.
Some studies assessed only the use and implementation of ABW spaces, not actual impacts.
Lack of clear descriptions of the former situation before ABW adoption in many reviewed papers.
Limited generalizability to other cultures, as most literature is from the Netherlands and a handful of other countries.
Most studies are from the corporate industry, with limited information about the public sector (where less positive outcomes are reported).
Lack of objective measures and evidence on health and health behavioural effects.
Health outcomes were often reported as 'overall health' rather than specific physical or mental health effects.
design_implications: ABW can support employees in working more collaboratively, with efficient and effective communication methods, through increased opportunities for formal and informal knowledge exchanges.
Workplaces should provide sufficient and well-designed workspaces for quiet/concentrated work to improve performance.
A thorough needs assessment should be conducted before construction or refurbishment to tailor ABW design to workers' specific needs (e.g., type of work, personalities).
The transition to an ABW environment must be accompanied by a revision of the organization's management style and support to foster job autonomy and flexibility.

Strategies need to be implemented to ensure private conversations can be held comfortably, and workstations should be designed to allow workers to be out of sight of others, emphasizing thoughtful design for privacy.
Flexible design based on needs assessment and an iterative process can improve function and satisfaction in ABW environments.
ABW can be promoted for its benefits in work performance and perceptions of the work environment when coupled with flexible design, appropriate management support, and organization.
